title: 020 Removing Stopped Containers

segments.text: In the last section, I had mentioned that I cleared out all the stopped containers on my machine,
and so I thought you might be curious on how I did that.
If I run Docker PS--all right now, I can see that I currently have two stopped containers.
So these containers right now are essentially just taking up this space on my computer.
And so it might be to my advantage to try to entirely delete them and not just leave them in this stop state.
To delete all these containers, I can run Docker System prune.
All then we presented with a warning here.
So just be clear, this is not only going to delete stopped containers,
it's also going to delete a couple of either items as well, most notably your build cache.
The build cache is any image that you have fetched from Docker Hub.
So after running Docker prune, you will have to redenload images from Docker Hub,
which is not a really big deal, just be aware that you're going to have to wait a couple minutes.
The next time you start up a container, not really a couple minutes, but a couple of seconds really.
So we can enter in, yes, hit enter, and then it will tell us about the deleted containers.
And I'll tell me also how much space has been reclaimed by deleting those resources.
If I then do another Docker PS-all, I'll see that I do not have any stopped containers whatsoever.
I really recommend you keep the Docker system prune command in mind,
because anytime that you're kind of done working with Docker for a period of weeks or months,
or if you decide you just don't want to work with Docker again at all,
you will want to run this command to delete any containers that are still just kind of sitting around,
eating up disk space.
